\chapter{Enye and the Upside-Down Marks}
\label{ch:enye-and-marks}
\hlchaptermodality{10}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can read and write ñ and the upside-down question and exclamation marks.}

Enye and the Upside-Down Marks — the chapter run end to end.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[ñ]{ñ — the letter that remembers a doubled n}

\label{lesson:ES-W02-enye}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{ñ} is the one letter English does not have — and it has the best origin story in the alphabet. That wavy hat (\texttt{\textasciitilde{}}, a \emph{tilde}) is not decoration. It is \textbf{a tiny second \emph{n}, written on top to save space.} Once you know that, you know both how to write it \emph{and} why it sounds as it does.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\textbf{ñ} = the \emph{ny} in \textquotedblleft{}ca\textbf{ny}on\textquotedblright{} or \textquotedblleft{}o\textbf{ni}on\textquotedblright{} — one squished sound, tongue flat against the roof of the mouth. English \emph{canyon} is, in fact, Spanish \textbf{cañón} with the \emph{ñ} spelled out as \emph{ny}. Say \textquotedblleft{}onion,\textquotedblright{} freeze on the middle: that is ñ.
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Script — how to write it}
Write a normal \textbf{n}, then a small wavy \textbf{\textasciitilde{}} floating above it. Two strokes, one letter.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Careful:} \textbf{ñ is its own letter}, not \textquotedblleft{}n with an accent.\textquotedblright{} \emph{año} (\textquotedblleft{}year\textquotedblright{}) and \emph{ano} (a rather different word) are completely different words — the tilde is not an optional flourish, it is a distinct letter of the alphabet, with its own slot in the dictionary.
\end{quote}

\begin{culture}
That wave is a \textbf{medieval shorthand}. Scribes copying Latin were forever writing double letters, so they saved a stroke: write the letter \textbf{once}, and put a little mark above meaning \emph{\textquotedblleft{}…and one more of these.\textquotedblright{}} A bar over a vowel meant a dropped \emph{n} or \emph{m} (Latin \emph{tantum} $\to$ \emph{tãtum}); a wave over an \emph{n} meant \textbf{nn}.

Spanish is full of words where a Latin \textbf{-nn-} did exactly this:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Latin \textbf{annus} (\textquotedblleft{}year\textquotedblright{}) $\to$ \emph{anno} $\to$ \textbf{año}. (That same \emph{annus} gives English \textbf{ann}ual, \textbf{ann}iversary, bi-\textbf{enn}ial.)
  \item Latin \textbf{canna} (\textquotedblleft{}reed\textquotedblright{}) $\to$ \textbf{caña}; Latin \emph{domina} $\to$ \emph{donna} $\to$ \textbf{doña}.
\end{itemize}

So the tilde on \textbf{ñ} is a \textbf{frozen abbreviation} — a thousand-year-old note saying \textquotedblleft{}there used to be two \emph{n}'s here.\textquotedblright{} You are writing a scribe's shortcut.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}año\textquotedblright{} — \emph{AH-nyo}, one squished \emph{ny}; then English \textquotedblleft{}annual\textquotedblright{}
  \item the doubled-n words — \textquotedblleft{}año, caña, doña\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is the tilde on \emph{ñ}, really? (A tiny second \emph{n} — a scribe's shorthand for a doubled \emph{nn}.) What Latin word gives \emph{año}, and what English words share it? (\emph{Annus} $\to$ annual, anniversary.) Is \emph{ñ} a separate letter or an accented \emph{n}? (A \textbf{separate letter}.) Next: the two everyday words you will be writing it in.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mañana, español]{mañana, español — the ñ in the words you are about to need}

\label{lesson:ES-W02-enye-formas}



\begin{quote}
You can write \textbf{ñ} and you can say it. Two of the next words in this book carry it, and both are worth a minute on their own — because neither of them got its \emph{ñ} from a doubled \emph{n}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item ñ — the letter, the sound, and the scribe's shorthand.
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Script — the two forms}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{mañana} — \textquotedblleft{}tomorrow,\textquotedblright{} and also \textquotedblleft{}morning.\textquotedblright{} \emph{ma-NYA-na}: the \emph{ñ} is in the \textbf{middle}, and it is the stressed syllable.
  \item \textbf{español} — \textquotedblleft{}Spanish.\textquotedblright{} \emph{es-pa-NYOL}: the \emph{ñ} is at the \textbf{end}, right before the \emph{-ol}.
\end{itemize}

Now the honest footnote. The scribe's doubled \emph{nn} is \textbf{one} road to \emph{ñ}, the one you met with \emph{año}. These two words took a \textbf{different} road: Latin's \textbf{-ni-} before a vowel. \emph{Mañana} traces back through \emph{maneana} to \textbf{māne} (\textquotedblleft{}morning\textquotedblright{} — the root of English \textbf{matinée}); \emph{español} comes from \textbf{Hispaniolus}, built on \textbf{Hispania}. In both, a \emph{ni} sequence squeezed together into the same single palatal sound.

So \emph{ñ} is where \textbf{two} separate Latin sequences ended up — \emph{-nn-} and \emph{-ni-}. One letter, one sound, two histories.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}año, mañana, español\textquotedblright{} — the ñ in three positions
  \item the two roads — \textquotedblleft{}año, from -nn-\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}mañana, from -ni-\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where does the \emph{ñ} sit in \emph{mañana}, and where in \emph{español}? (Middle; end.) Did those two get their \emph{ñ} from a doubled \emph{n}? (\textbf{No} — from Latin \textbf{-ni-} before a vowel, a second road to the same letter.) What was the first road? (\textbf{-nn-}, the scribe's shorthand, as in \emph{año}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[¿ ¡]{¿ ¡ — the marks that open a question}

\label{lesson:ES-W03-inverted}



\begin{quote}
You've been writing them since \emph{¿cómo está usted?} Spanish is the one major language that puts an \textbf{upside-down} question or exclamation mark at the \textbf{start} of the sentence, as well as the normal one at the end. It looks exotic; the reason is purely practical.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — the two opening marks}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{¿ … ?} wraps a question: \emph{¿Cómo estás?}
  \item \textbf{¡ … !} wraps an exclamation: \emph{¡Hola!} \emph{¡Gracias!}
\end{itemize}

The opening mark is just the closing mark \textbf{flipped 180°} — turned upside down \emph{and} left-right. To write \textbf{¿}, draw a normal \emph{?} and rotate it half a turn: the hook ends up at the bottom, the dot on top.

\begin{culture}
English lets you read most of a sentence before the final \textbf{?} reveals it was a question — fine, because English usually flags a question early with word order (\textquotedblleft{}\emph{Are} you…\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}\emph{Do} you…\textquotedblright{}). Spanish often \textbf{doesn't reorder words}: \emph{Tienes hambre.} (\textquotedblleft{}You're hungry.\textquotedblright{}) and \emph{¿Tienes hambre?} (\textquotedblleft{}Are you hungry?\textquotedblright{}) are the \textbf{same words} — only punctuation and the spoken rising tone tell them apart.

So the Spanish Royal Academy, in \textbf{1754}, made the opening \textbf{¿} official: it warns the reader \emph{\textquotedblleft{}a question is starting — read this with rising intonation from the very first word.\textquotedblright{}} It's a \textbf{melody cue placed before the melody}, the exact same instinct as the written accent marking stress you can't otherwise see. For a language read aloud, it's genuinely useful.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item read \textquotedblleft{}¿Cómo estás?\textquotedblright{} — start the rising \emph{question} melody from the very first word, the way the ¿ tells you to
  \item \textquotedblleft{}¡Hola!\textquotedblright{} — the ¡ warns you to begin with exclamation energy
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Why does Spanish open a question with \textbf{¿}? (Because word order often doesn't change, so the reader needs an early warning to use question intonation.) How do you write it? (A normal \emph{?} rotated 180°.) Does it always sit at the sentence's start? (\textbf{The next step places it around a question inside a larger sentence.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Roberto, ¿cómo estás?]{Where does ¿ begin? — bracket the spoken span}

\label{lesson:ES-W03-question-span}



\begin{quote}
You can open a whole question with \textbf{¿}. Now place that mark inside a larger sentence, exactly where the questioning voice begins.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — bracket the spoken span}
The opening mark goes where the \textbf{question} begins, even if the sentence started earlier:

\begin{quote}
Roberto, \textbf{¿cómo estás?}
\end{quote}

The name \textbf{Roberto} is outside the question. The marks bracket the words that need question intonation. The same principle works for an exclamation:

\begin{quote}
Roberto, \textbf{¡buenos días!}
\end{quote}

This is why the opening mark is more than decoration. It tells the reader exactly where to begin and end a change in spoken melody.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} “María, ¿cómo estás?”
  \item \emph{Write it:} “María, ¡buenos días!”
  \item \emph{Say it:} begin the new melody at ¿ or ¡, not at the first capital
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
In \textbf{Roberto, ¿cómo estás?}, is \textbf{Roberto} inside the question? (\textbf{No.}) Where does the inverted mark go? (\textbf{At the start of the question or exclamation span.}) What does that placement tell a reader? (\textbf{Where to change the spoken melody.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Practice — \textquotedblleft{}how are you?\textquotedblright{}, start to finish}

\label{lesson:ES-C04-practice}



\begin{quote}
No new words. This chapter's atoms — \emph{gracias, de nada, estar, ¿cómo está?, regular} — now assemble into a real exchange, run formally and informally until the register swap is automatic. It picks up right where the introduction left off.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The exchange}
\textbf{Formal} (a stranger, an elder, a customer):

\begin{quote}
— Buenos días. ¿\textbf{Cómo está usted}? — \textbf{Bien, gracias.} ¿Y usted? — \textbf{Más o menos.} — {[}reply to a thanks, later in the chat{]} \textbf{De nada.}
\end{quote}

\textbf{Informal} (a friend, a peer) — only the verb + pronoun change:

\begin{quote}
— ¡Hola! ¿\textbf{Cómo estás}? — \textbf{Regular.} ¿Y tú? — Bien, gracias.
\end{quote}

The glue pattern you just secured is \textbf{¿y usted? / ¿y tú?} — “and you?” It bounces the question back without repeating the whole sentence.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built this chapter}]
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{gracias} — thank you ($\leftarrow$ \emph{grātia}, \textquotedblleft{}grace\textquotedblright{}).
  \item \textbf{de nada} — you're welcome ($\leftarrow$ \textquotedblleft{}of a born-thing\textquotedblright{} $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}of nothing\textquotedblright{}).
  \item \textbf{estar} — the state/location be-verb ($\leftarrow$ \emph{stāre}, “to stand”).
  \item \textbf{¿cómo está usted? / ¿cómo estás?} — how are you, formal / informal.
  \item \textbf{bien / regular / más o menos} — well / so-so / more-or-less.
\end{itemize}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the full \emph{formal} exchange, both voices
  \item the same exchange \emph{informally} — catch \emph{está $\to$ estás}, \emph{usted $\to$ tú}
  \item chain the two — introduce yourself \emph{and} ask how they are: \textquotedblleft{}Me llamo … ¿Cómo está usted?\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} Run the formal exchange, greeting to answer, without stopping.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which be-verb carries \textquotedblleft{}how are you?\textquotedblright{} and why? (\emph{estar} — current state.) Two words swap between formal and informal — which? (\emph{está $\to$ estás}, and \emph{usted $\to$ tú}.) What does \emph{de nada} literally say? (\textquotedblleft{}Of nothing.\textquotedblright{}) And if the person answering you says \textbf{vos} instead of \emph{tú} — do you switch? (\emph{No. You understand it and keep saying tú.}) Next chapter: \textbf{farewells} — hasta luego, hasta mañana, adiós.
\end{tcolorbox}
